look_here_first: CROP SORGHUM (S. bicolor): generally ANNUAL, robust erect cane-like culms, broad flat leaf blades and upright crop/forage PANICLES of widely VARIABLE tightness. The individual Sorghum inflorescence units include a fertile sessile spikelet and a pedicelled partner; examine attachments and grain glumes under 10–20×. Distinguish Johnsongrass S. halepense by its deep CREEPING SCALY RHIZOMES and perennial colonies, not by red-purple panicle or pale blade stripe. Shattercane feral forms of S. bicolor may shatter ripe seed and resemble Johnsongrass: a mature seedhead or vegetative view by itself is NOT definitive.

field_sequence: Recognize: robust erect grass with broad flat leaves, often showing a pale midrib, and a terminal panicle of short flowering branches.
Look closer: inspect the leaf collar for the ligule and the flowering branches for paired spikelets; a distant panicle photo cannot resolve these.
Confirm against Johnsongrass: established S. halepense is a perennial spreading via thick scaly underground rhizomes; cultivated S. bicolor usually lacks this rhizomatous system.

Shattercane is a weedy form within the S. bicolor complex, not automatically a distinct species. Examine mature grain shattering and agricultural context; color and open-versus-compact heads alone are insufficient.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Whole crop or escape clump with the actual fibrous or rooted base, 1-cm scale
True collar and membranous ligule at 10×
One intact sessile and pedicelled spikelet pair with mm ruler
Mature S. bicolor grain and bracts, examine shattering under permitted field conditions
Side-by-side actual Johnsongrass rhizome and mature seed/spikelet pair

comparisons.key_distinctions: Johnsongrass (S. halepense): persistent scaly underground rhizomes in established plants. Shattercane: weedy S. bicolor forms that shed mature grain more readily than most domesticated grain sorghum; panicle compactness varies and cannot reliably distinguish them.

measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.look_here_first: CROP SORGHUM / SHATTERCANE: confirm a large annual or short-lived nonrhizomatous Sorghum with a compound panicle. At a terminal raceme, locate one sessile bisexual spikelet paired with a smaller pedicelled staminate/sterile spikelet. To separate Johnsongrass, expose the actual basal crown and search for scaly creeping rhizomes; panicle color, white midrib and awn presence are insufficient.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.measured_growth_collar: FNA: culms 50–500+ cm, sometimes tillering; annual or short-lived perennial WITHOUT rhizomes. Leaf blades 5–100 mm wide; true membranous ligule 1–4 mm; no auricles (Go Botany). Cultivated height and blade width vary markedly; avoid making either an absolute identification threshold.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.measured_panicle_pair: FNA: compound panicles 5–60 cm long and 3–30 cm wide; terminal rames with 2–7 sessile/pedicelled spikelet pairs. Sessile bisexual spikelet 3–9 mm; pedicelled usually staminate or sterile, 3–6 mm on a 1–2.6 mm pedicel. Measure BOTH partners while still attached to a branchlet; do not confuse pedicel with rachis internode.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.glume_lemma_awn_anatomy: The sessile fertile spikelet bears two glumes that typically enclose the florets: lower glume generally with two marginal keels, upper with one apical keel (USDA IDtools). A basal sterile lemma is separate from the fertile upper lemma. Fertile upper lemma thin/hyaline, reported 1–5 mm in USDA IDtools; its apex may be entire or lobed, unawned or bearing one bent/twisted awn 5–30 mm (FNA). The AWN arises from the fertile lemma, NOT from a glume; awnlessness is possible in cultivated plants. FNA glumes vary from leathery to membranous and hairless to hairy, so texture/hair alone cannot certify a cultivar.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.local_lookalikes: S. halepense (introduced Johnsongrass) persists as a rhizomatous perennial with scaly creeping underground stems; S. bicolor generally lacks rhizomes and may be cultivated or feral. Shattercane is a shattering form of S. bicolor, NOT a separate confirmed species: inspect mature grain attachment and spontaneous shedding, but do not assume all crop sorghum shatters. Corn (Zea mays) has a different reproductive architecture, with tassels and ears instead of the terminal sorghum grain panicle.
precise_photo_arrow_holds: Same exact-species rooted crop/feral plant: expose intact fibrous crown and verify ABSENCE of rhizomes, with 1-cm scale; do not infer from cut stem.
Actual blade–sheath junction with 1-mm scale and 10× view showing 1–4 mm membranous ligule, collar and absence of auricles.
Intact terminal raceme segment with 2–7 pairs and 1-mm scale: arrow separately to sessile fertile spikelet, pedicelled reduced spikelet, pedicel and rachis segment.

Detached mature sessile spikelet in face/edge views, 10–20×, show two enclosing glumes, basal sterile lemma, upper fertile lemma and variable 0 or 5–30 mm fertile-lemma awn; only place arrows after exact structures visible.
Source-verified mature shattercane versus crop sorghum grain attachment, and separately a real Johnsongrass scaly rhizome; no unlicensed comparison images.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Sorghum — leaf collar then sessile/pedicelled spikelet pairs
steps: Find the actual branched terminal sorghum panicle attached to a broad-leaved culm: dense crop or loose feral heads are both possible.
Open the real ligule photo: follow blade into sheath, locating the membrane. A source close-up without 1-mm scale does not prove actual ligule length.
Examine the flowering branch close-up: identify potential paired units but don't confuse whole spikelets with exposed anthers or stigmas.
Use an intact mature raceme under a lens: one sessile fertile and one pedicelled staminate/sterile spikelet normally accompany each other; a measured same-specimen photograph remains missing.
Dig only where permitted: true Johnsongrass has scaly creeping rhizomes; S. bicolor does not. Do not conclude lack of rhizomes from a cropped culm photo.
Compare mature attached or shattering grain separately. Shattercane is a shattering form within S. bicolor; head color or one awn cannot reliably name the form.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Whole panicle + real collar + attached sessile/pedicelled units + verified basal growth; never declare S. bicolor versus S. halepense on seedhead silhouette alone.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: All 3 exact-species images are physically archived. Rasbak anatomy photos were missing from visual_comparison and are now linked; no microscopic structures calibrated and no new arrows fabricated.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
field_id_short_tiles.short: Robust annual Sorghum; verify the actual base and paired spikelets
field_id_short_tiles.details: Crop sorghum and escaped shattercane have broad leaves and terminal panicles varying from tightly packed grain heads to open branched heads. Trace the rooted annual crown, then inspect a branchlet for a larger sessile fertile spikelet beside a stalked companion. White midrib, grain color and head compactness are NOT species-proof.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FIELD-READY GROSS CUE; CONNECTED BASE NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · CHECK THE ROOTS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Typically no long scaly rhizomes; Johnsongrass has them
field_id_short_tiles.details: Flora of North America describes S. bicolor as annual or short-lived perennial, generally without rhizomes, with culms 50–500+ cm. In established S. halepense colonies, look for persistent jointed creeping underground rhizomes. The existing rhizome comparison panel depicts OTHER SPECIES Johnsongrass, not S. bicolor. Do not infer absence of rhizomes from a cut stem.
field_id_short_tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — CONNECTED S. BICOLOR ROOTED CROWN

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · OPEN THE TRUE COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Membranous ligule about 1–4 mm; no auricles
field_id_short_tiles.details: At the inner blade–sheath junction find the actual membranous ligule, approximately 1–4 mm in published FNA treatment, and check for absent auricles. The Rasbak S. bicolor collar photograph is archived as panel 2, but it is not millimeter-calibrated; do not arrow an unverified membrane edge or substitute the S. halepense comparison collar.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · EXAMINE A PAIRED SPIKELET UNIT
field_id_short_tiles.short: Sessile fertile spikelet 3–9 mm; pedicelled partner 3–6 mm
field_id_short_tiles.details: Published FNA ranges: compound panicle 5–60 cm, branchlet with 2–7 sessile/pedicelled pairs; fertile sessile spikelet ~3–9 mm, pedicelled often staminate or sterile ~3–6 mm on a 1–2.6 mm stalk. Photograph a connected mature pair at 10–20× with a 1-mm ruler. Panel 3 shows actual S. bicolor flowers but does not independently establish all attachment points.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · DISSECT GLUMES AND LEMMA
field_id_short_tiles.short: Two enclosing glumes; upper fertile lemma may be awnless or bear a 5–30 mm awn
field_id_short_tiles.details: On one mature sessile spikelet separate the two enclosing glumes from the lower sterile lemma and the thin upper fertile lemma. Published USDA/FNA treatments describe the upper lemma as roughly 1–5 mm, varying from awnless to one bent/twisted awn about 5–30 mm. An awn arises from the lemma, NOT a glume. Awn presence and glume hairiness vary among cultivated and feral forms; the current gallery has no scale-verified dissection.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · RULE OUT JOHNSONGRASS AND SHATTERCANE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Rhizomatous perennial versus nonrhizomatous crop/feral annual; grain shattering varies
field_id_short_tiles.details: Johnsongrass (S. halepense) forms persistent perennial patches from scaly rhizomes. Feral shattercane belongs to the S. bicolor complex and may shed mature grains readily; cultivated grain sorghum often retains them. Neither purple color, pale leaf stripe, loose head nor shattering alone reliably separates all forms. Compare the actual crown and mature paired spikelets before a species-level determination.
